text: On September 5, 1977, a small spacecraft left Earth carrying something far bigger than its size suggested: a message from humanity.

label: A MESSAGE FROM HUMANITY
asset: nasa_image:Voyager Golden Record gold-plated disc carried on Voyager 1

text: It was Voyager 1, launched on a trajectory designed to visit the giant planets of the outer Solar System.

asset: nasa_image:Voyager 1 launch atop its Titan Centaur rocket in 1977

text: Its journey would eventually take it farther from the Sun than any human-made object had ever gone. First came Jupiter.
FARTHER THAN ANY HUMAN-MADE OBJECT

In 1979, Voyager 1 swept past the largest planet in our Solar System, capturing detailed images of its enormous storms and discovering previously unknown features, including a thin ring and two new moons.

label: ENORMOUS STORMS
asset: nasa_image:Voyager 1 view of the Jupiter Great Red Spot and its storms

text: Then the spacecraft continued toward Saturn. In 1980, Voyager 1 passed Saturn and made a close encounter with its giant moon Titan.

label: TITAN
asset: nasa_image:Voyager 1 photograph of Titan and its orange haze

text: That encounter changed everything. Gravity from Saturn redirected Voyager 1 onto a path that would carry it outward, away from the plane of the planets and toward the edge of the Sun’s influence.
AWAY FROM THE PLANE OF THE PLANETS
But the planetary tour was only the beginning. For more than two decades, Voyager 1 crossed an increasingly distant and unfamiliar region of space.

asset: nasa_image:Voyager 1 Family Portrait mosaic of the planets taken from the edge of the Solar System in 1990

text: In December 2004, after traveling about 94 times the distance between Earth and the Sun, it crossed the termination shock, where the solar wind suddenly slowed and became turbulent.
THE TERMINATION SHOCK
Then came the heliosheath, the outer region of the Sun’s enormous bubble. On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 finally crossed the heliopause at about 122 astronomical units from the Sun.
THE HELIOSHEATH

label: THE SUN'S BUBBLE
asset: nasa_image:NASA illustration of the heliosphere bubble around the Sun with the heliosheath and heliopause

text: THE HELIOPAUSE: AUGUST 25, 2012
For the first time, a human-made spacecraft had entered interstellar space. And Voyager did not find an empty void.

asset: nasa_image:artist concept of Voyager 1 entering interstellar space beyond the heliopause

text: Its instruments began measuring particles and magnetic fields from the space between stars, giving humanity its first direct measurements from beyond the Sun’s protective bubble.

label: ITS INSTRUMENTS
asset: nasa_image:graphic of the Voyager 1 spacecraft and the location of its instrument

text: FIRST DIRECT MEASUREMENTS
Voyager 1 began as a mission to explore Jupiter and Saturn. But its real destination became something much larger. The space between the stars.
